description: Single source for architecture arrows, flow messages, code references, language and deployment. Generated assets must not be edited by hand.

components.name: Customer / operations UI
components.scaling: No background polling. Bounded API lists, manual refresh.

community.explanation: The bank app or website is the customer-facing part of Nexo’s browser UI. Nexo also adds an operations view for batches and delivery attempts; this reference does not draw that view.

Frontend is the closest match to Nexo’s customer UI. Nexo also provides an operations view. The reference discusses internal clients, while Nexo authorizes each customer to see only their own disputes.

components.name: Chargeback API

sources.label: Reject extra requests when all 200 slots are busy

components.scaling: Add API replicas to handle more requests. Each pod allows 200 API requests at once; extra requests get HTTP 429 and Retry-After: 1. This keeps work from piling up at the database connection pool. Request bodies are limited to 4 KiB.

community.explanation: Nexo’s Go API combines chargeback validation and request handling with authentication, authorization and request limits. The reference separates those responsibilities into a chargeback service and an API gateway. Kubernetes routes traffic to API replicas.

The chargeback service and API gateway together cover Nexo’s Go API. Nexo handles authentication, customer ownership, request limits and idempotent creation in that one service; it does not deploy a separate gateway.

components.name: PostgreSQL + work queue
components.scaling: Four logical partitions; eligibility and due-work indexes. Physical sharding is not implemented. Managed cloud PostgreSQL is proposed, not provisioned.

community.explanation: Nexo keeps the relational database role and stores pending work in the same PostgreSQL tables. Eligible chargeback rows and due batch rows replace the work handoffs shown through Kafka. Nexo does not implement Kafka, change data capture or a replayable event stream. Audit records are written in the same database transaction.

Nexo combines the Database and Delivery queue roles in PostgreSQL: a pending chargeback waits for a batch, and a due batch waits for a worker. The reference also uses Kafka to absorb incoming bursts. Nexo instead uses durable rows and API request limits; it does not provide Kafka’s independent event stream.

components.name: Four daily slots
components.scaling: 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 and 18:00 UTC. Replays share durable slot and assignment records.

community.explanation: Both designs use a scheduled trigger four times per day. Nexo’s Kubernetes CronJob starts a bounded build Job for the intended UTC cutoff. PostgreSQL records the slot so a replay resumes the same work.

Both designs separate the clock from delivery. This reference schedules ready files for sending; Nexo’s CronJob claims and builds files for each cutoff, then delivery workers pick up ready batches. Nexo allows multiple bounded files in each of four daily windows, rather than at most four files per day.

components.name: Claim and build CSV
components.scaling: BATCH_MAX_ROWS limits rows per file; SCHEDULE_MAX_BATCHES limits new batches per run. A database lock allows one active scheduler.

community.explanation: Nexo’s Python Job covers the batch manager and file export workers, plus the finalizer’s file-building responsibility. It claims a bounded set of rows, writes one immutable CSV per batch and archives it. Nexo does not split one batch into chunk files or merge those chunks; delivery is a separate worker.

The Batch builder worker is the same role: atomically claim chargebacks, preserve membership and order, generate a CSV and save its identity. Nexo runs this Python code as a bounded Kubernetes Job and starts it from the scheduled slot, without a Kafka consumer.

components.name: CSV artifact storage
components.scaling: The batch ID determines the object key. Files are limited to 10,000 rows / 4 MiB. SeaweedFS runs locally; cloud object storage has not been provisioned.

community.explanation: Both archive the final immutable CSV in object storage. This reference also stores intermediate chunk files; Nexo creates a bounded final file directly. Nexo uses the S3 protocol with SeaweedFS locally and planned DigitalOcean Spaces in the cloud.

The S3 archive corresponds to Nexo’s immutable CSV storage. The batch records its object key, byte count and SHA-256 digest so the delivery worker can verify and resend the same bytes when safe. Nexo uses S3-compatible storage, not necessarily the AWS service.

components.name: Delivery worker
components.scaling: Each process handles one transfer at a time and reads up to 20 due batches. More replicas can handle different batches; a database lock prevents two workers handling the same batch.

community.explanation: Nexo’s Go worker covers the finalizer’s transfer responsibility and the part of reconciliation that checks file acknowledgements. It does not merge chunk files or decide the customer’s dispute. It retries the same batch identity, checks remote evidence and preserves unknown outcomes when submission cannot be proved.

Delivery Worker is the same role: read the archived CSV, send it over SFTP and record each attempt. Nexo polls durable batch rows instead of a separate delivery queue, and reads acknowledgement files instead of receiving the reference’s HTTP callback.

components.name: Visa / Mastercard simulator
components.scaling: One receiver with persistent volume and SQLite receipts. This is a simulator, not card-network certification.

community.explanation: This is the external card-network boundary. Nexo substitutes a clearly labeled Visa/Mastercard simulator using real SFTP and a documented teaching CSV and acknowledgement contract. It does not connect to actual card networks or implement their proprietary formats.

External Payment Network is the boundary simulated by Nexo. The simulator accepts Visa and Mastercard files over real SFTP, preserves receipts and can trigger delivery failures. Its CSV and acknowledgement formats are teaching contracts, not card-network certification.

requirements.title: File a chargeback and check its status.
requirements.explanation: A provisioned customer uses the real customer page to see imported transactions, dispute an owned transaction and read its status. Customer identity, network and currency come from server-side records. The same customer, idempotency key and request return the same chargeback; changed content returns 409, and different keys cannot dispute the same transaction twice.
requirements.limitation: Transactions are synthetic imports. One chargeback per transaction is an initial scope limit. Acknowledgement confirms the receiver’s answer, not settlement or a refund.

requirements.title: Send CSVs to each network in four daily slots.
requirements.explanation: At 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 and 18:00 UTC, a Kubernetes CronJob launches bounded batch work. Missed slots can be replayed. A slot claims committed, eligible, unassigned requests received before its cutoff; late commits wait for a later slot. Batch work writes comma-separated values (CSV) files split by network and stable logical partition, with a configurable row cap. It stores immutable objects through S3-compatible storage and delivers them over SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol). A matching durable acknowledgement sets acknowledged or rejected. Without it, a published batch stays submitted or unknown; a mismatched file identity, hash or row count becomes an observable conflict.
requirements.limitation: Four daily submission windows can contain multiple bounded files. The user approved SFTP and the simulator contract on 2026-10-05; this is not a proprietary Visa/Mastercard file format or a live network integration.

requirements.title: Never put a chargeback in two submitted files.
requirements.explanation: PostgreSQL transactions, uniqueness constraints and immutable-membership triggers assign each chargeback permanently to at most one batch, including under concurrency. Each batch has one deterministic CSV and final filename. The worker uploads to a unique temporary name, verifies its bytes, commits publication intent, then renames without replacing an existing final file. A retry checks the acknowledgement and original final file first; reconciliation never creates a new batch. The simulator keeps durable, unique file and chargeback receipts.
requirements.limitation: SFTP alone does not provide exactly-once delivery. Once publication may have occurred, a missing final file does not prove failure: without receiver evidence, Nexo keeps unknown and does not publish again.

requirements.title: Inspect batches, files and delivery attempts.
requirements.explanation: The operations page calls the real service and requires an operations role. It shows lifecycle counts, queue age, batches, immutable file digests, delivery attempts and audit events, so accepted work can be followed through its recorded outcome.
requirements.limitation: This is a small operations view with manual refresh and bounded recent lists, not a full observability stack.

requirements.title: Preserve exact amounts and identities.
requirements.explanation: Amounts are positive integer minor units expressed as decimal strings at the HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) boundary and stored as PostgreSQL bigint; they never pass through floating point. An amount cannot exceed the original transaction. Server-side ownership checks and database constraints preserve transaction and chargeback identities. Batch membership and the stored file manifest remain fixed, and generated rows preserve the recorded amounts and identifiers.
requirements.limitation: Nexo submits disputes; it does not move money, convert currencies, settle refunds or implement a general payment ledger.

requirements.title: Keep accepted work durable and auditable.
requirements.explanation: No accepted write is acknowledged before its database commit. Each accepted chargeback links to an append-only audit event, each delivery attempt has a durable record, and stored CSV artifacts and receiver receipts preserve evidence across process restarts. PostgreSQL currently holds the durable work queue. Database backups and restore exercises are part of deployment readiness.
requirements.limitation: The local restore drill covers a small PostgreSQL snapshot, not object storage, receiver files or cloud recovery. Cross-store disaster recovery is manual. Kafka is not implemented; its hosting choice is still pending.

requirements.title: Keep work bounded as volume grows.
requirements.explanation: Batch row caps, bounded database reads, worker concurrency, finite connection pools, request body limits and network timeouts bound work and memory. Logical partitions allow independent claimers. The initial targets are 100 accepted requests/second and 100,000 chargebacks drained within six hours. The recorded local run accepted 1,000 requests at 506.7/second in a short burst and drained 100,000 already accepted fixtures through matching acknowledgements in 48.93 seconds.
requirements.limitation: The intake sample lasted about two seconds; the 100,000-row backlog was seeded separately. These measurements are not sustained throughput, Kubernetes workload sizing, cloud capacity or bank-scale validation. Physical database sharding is not implemented.

requirements.title: Restrict access and protect customer data.
requirements.explanation: Revocable opaque bearer tokens identify customers and operations roles; the database stores token hashes. Requests enforce ownership, strict field validation, parameterized queries and safe errors. Logs exclude tokens and customer payloads, and Nexo never receives a card number. Credentials and Secure Shell (SSH) host keys are generated outside version control; the worker verifies the receiver’s host key. Production transport must be encrypted.
requirements.limitation: Identity-provider integration is not implemented. Local loopback HTTP and unencrypted local database connections are documented exceptions. Local network policies are not enforced by default kind networking; cloud enforcement still needs verification. No bank security certification is claimed.

requirements.title: Run the same workloads locally and in cloud.
requirements.explanation: The service and delivery worker use Kubernetes Deployments; the scheduler launches bounded CronJob Jobs, and migrations use a Job. Shared base manifests support local kind and cloud overlays, with the simulator in a separate namespace. Local Kubernetes runs these workloads. The user approved DigitalOcean managed Kubernetes, managed PostgreSQL and Spaces on 2026-10-05.
requirements.limitation: Cloud resources have not been provisioned. Provisioning still requires user sign-in and approval of the concrete resource plan, topology and cost. This is a single-region learning system, without multi-region failover.
